parsed.modern: Where fenestence could wish the word with which it began, it is called _spanialphs_. As in that expression of Phants, « Virtue contains all things, he wants no good thing who likes virtue." The figure is the same, but the principle not so honorable, in the advice which we find given by the miler in Horace, when he says, "Get money if you can, possibly, but however, get money." This figure adds a force to an expression, when the principal thing designed to be conveyed is thus repeated, by leaving it fall upon the mind. And it heightens the beauty of it, when the fenestone has an agreeable turn arising from two opposite parts. As in Cicero's compliment to Caesar: "We have few your colony remained by the way, your own lived in the city we have not feen." Hermogenes calls this a circle, because the fenestence returns again to the same word, as that geometrical figure is formed by the orbicular motion of a line to the same point.
